questions.q: What two axes does this lesson use to prioritize which risks should actually shape a design?
options: Cost and schedule
Technical complexity and team size
Client seniority and panel size
Likelihood and impact
questions.explain: Sorting by how likely a risk is and how bad it would be if it occurred is what separates risks that must visibly shape the design from ones that only need a brief acknowledgment.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why does Nimbus Mobile's design (Lesson 6) treat outage alerts as a separate event-driven push rather than routing them through the ordinary customer-interaction queue?
options: Because routing-system overload during a real regional outage is both likely to eventually happen and high-impact to customers mid-crisis, so it needs to visibly shape the design
Because outage alerts are low-likelihood and low-impact, so they don't need special handling
Because Omni-Channel technically cannot process more than one type of work item
Because event-driven architecture is always required for every telecom scenario regardless of risk
questions.explain: This is a risk that scores high on both likelihood and impact, which is exactly why it gets dedicated design treatment rather than a passing mention.

questions.q: What is the distinguishing feature of a "delivery risk," as opposed to a technical or business risk?
options: Whether the solution works correctly once built
Whether the team can actually build and ship the solution within the given timeframe and resources
Whether the organization's reputation or customers are harmed even if the build succeeds technically
Whether the panel approves of the chosen cloud product
questions.explain: Delivery risk is specifically about the team's ability to build and ship on time — Meridian Outfitters' nine-month deadline is a delivery risk even for a design that already avoids the riskiest technical path.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a defensible design shouldn't try to eliminate every identified risk down to zero?
options: Because eliminating risk is against Salesforce's platform terms of service
Because risks that are named out loud automatically disappear

Because the actual standard is that the highest-priority risks are addressed by specific design choices while lower-priority risks are named and consciously accepted, not silently ignored or over-engineered against
Because every risk should be assigned to the client to solve, not the architect
questions.explain: Trying to engineer every risk to zero isn't realistic or expected — the standard is proportionate response: address what matters most, consciously accept the rest.

questions.q: In Carrow Equipment's design (Lesson 4), how does the design respond to the residual risk that a live Salesforce Connect query to SAP could be slow during SAP's peak load?
options: By acknowledging the risk and proposing a proportionate response (a loading state in the order UX) rather than a bigger architectural investment
By abandoning Salesforce Connect entirely and replicating all pricing data instead
By ignoring the risk completely since it's unlikely to ever occur
By requiring SAP to guarantee zero downtime through a legal contract
questions.explain: This is the lesson's example of consciously accepting a real-but-not-severe risk with a proportionate response, instead of either ignoring it or over-investing to eliminate it entirely.
